items.question: According to AW139 AFCS limitations, how should upper modes be used following a single autopilot (AP) failure?
options: All upper modes may be used normally.
Upper modes must be disengaged except those specifically permitted by the AFCS limitations.
HOV and TDH modes must be engaged immediately.
Only GA/TU mode may be used.
items.explanation: AFCS limitations restrict upper mode use following failures; pilots must comply with the RFM limitations after an AP failure.

items.question: Is intentional pitch/roll (P/R) or collective/yaw (C/Y) trim de-clutching during flight (using the EDCU TRIM page) allowed on the AW139?
options: Yes, in all phases of flight.
Yes, but only during hover.
No, intentional trim de-clutching in flight is prohibited.
Only above 100 KIAS.
items.explanation: Intentional trim de-clutching in flight is prohibited in many AFCS installations; the AW139 AFCS limitations reflect this restriction.

items.question: When is use of AFCS GA/TU (Go Around/Takeoff) mode generally approved on the AW139?
options: Only for VFR day flights.
For go-around or takeoff in accordance with AFCS and performance limitations.
Only on the ground.
It is not an approved mode in normal operations.
items.explanation: GA/TU is an operational mode intended for go-around/takeoff when used within AFCS and performance limitations.

items.question: What is a general requirement before using coupled AFCS approaches in the AW139?
options: Both autopilots and required sensors must be operative and the approach must be approved for coupled operation.
Only one AP is required.
AFCS must be off before the final segment.
No specific requirements; any approach may be flown coupled.
items.explanation: Coupled approaches require both APs and necessary sensors to be operative and the procedure to be approved for coupled flight.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 1/2  AFCS Coupled Approaches

items.question: Which crew action is required before engaging any AFCS upper mode in the AW139?
options: Verify AFCS is OFF.
Verify basic flight instruments, trim and flight controls are correctly set and no relevant AFCS cautions are present.
Pull all AFCS circuit breakers.
Set all NAV radios to OFF.
items.explanation: Engaging upper modes requires stable basic flight instrument indications, correctly set trim/controls, and absence of AFCS-related cautions.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2  AFCS Operating Procedures

items.question: What is a general requirement regarding use of Flight Director (FD) modes on the AW139?
options: FD modes may be engaged regardless of AFCS status.
FD modes should be used only when AFCS and trim systems are operating normally and crew is familiar with the mode behaviour.
FD modes must never be used in IFR.
FD modes may be used only in hover.
items.explanation: Use of FD modes assumes correctly functioning AFCS/trim and crew understanding of mode behaviour and limitations.

items.question: After an AFCS malfunction on the AW139, when is re-engagement of upper modes typically allowed?
options: Immediately, without any checks.
Only after the cause is understood, the system is reset where permitted, and no relevant cautions remain.
Only above 10 000 ft.
Upper modes may never be used again on that flight.
items.explanation: Following a malfunction, re-engagement is only considered once the system has been correctly reset and indications confirm normal status within limitations.

items.question: What is a general EASA requirement for the use of RNAV (GNSS) approaches with the AW139 FMS?
options: They may be flown without any specific equipment approval.
They require suitable and approved GNSS/FMS equipment, database currency and crew training.
They may be flown with VFR-only equipment.
They are prohibited for helicopters.
items.explanation: RNAV approaches require approved equipment, up-to-date databases and appropriate crew training under EASA rules.

items.question: Before using GPS-based navigation in IFR with the AW139, what must the crew verify?
options: That the GPS antenna is painted red.
That the navigation database is current and the system status indicates proper operation.
That the fuel quantity is full.
That the rotor brake is set.
items.explanation: Use of GPS for IFR navigation requires a current navigation database and normal system status indications.

items.question: What is the purpose of the RA (radio altimeter) in instrument approaches with the AW139?
options: To measure outside air temperature.
To provide height above ground information, particularly useful for decision height and low-level operations.
To measure fuel quantity.
To drive the rotor brake.
items.explanation: The radio altimeter gives precise height above terrain, important for DH/DA and low-level procedures.

items.question: Which statement best describes the use of autopilot-coupled ILS approaches in the AW139?
options: They are never permitted.
They are permitted when the AFCS, ILS system and required redundancy meet the limitations in the RFM and AFM supplements.
They may be flown with the AFCS off.
They may be flown without glideslope information.
items.explanation: Coupled ILS approaches are allowed only when aircraft systems and redundancy meet the specified limitations and approvals.

items.question: In which flight phase should the crew be particularly cautious when changing AFCS modes in the AW139?
options: During cruise in smooth air only.
During critical phases such as take-off, approach and landing.
Only on the ground.
Mode changes are equally safe in all phases.
items.explanation: Mode changes in critical phases require extra attention to avoid unexpected aircraft responses.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – AFCS Operating Techniques

items.question: What is an important crew responsibility regarding FMS entries before flight in the AW139?
options: No verification is required.
Verify route, waypoints, altitudes and performance data for correctness before use.
Enter only departure aerodrome.
Let ATC upload the route remotely.
items.explanation: Crew must verify that all FMS entries are correct and reasonable before they are used for navigation or performance calculations.
references: EASA Air Ops – Use of FMS

items.question: When using the AW139 FMS for performance calculations, what must be ensured?
options: That the helicopter is empty.
That the database and performance software are applicable to the specific helicopter configuration and weight limits.
That only standard atmosphere is considered.
That icing conditions are ignored.
items.explanation: Performance tools must be applicable to the actual helicopter configuration and within approved weight/CG limits.

items.question: What is a limitation regarding use of weather radar on the AW139?
options: It may be used as the sole means of collision avoidance.
It should not be used for terrain clearance without appropriate terrain functions and procedures.
It is prohibited in IMC.
It may replace all visual lookout.
items.explanation: Conventional weather radar is not a primary terrain clearance device and must not replace required terrain avoidance procedures.

items.question: What does a TAWS/HTAWS caution typically indicate to the AW139 crew?
options: Engine oil over-temperature.
A predicted proximity to terrain/obstacles requiring crew attention and possible corrective action.
Overspeed of main rotor.
Low hydraulic quantity.
items.explanation: TAWS/HTAWS cautions signal potential terrain/obstacle conflicts based on current flight path.

items.question: When a TCAS/ACAS RA (Resolution Advisory) is issued during IFR flight in the AW139, what is the pilot's primary obligation?
options: Ignore the RA and follow ATC only.
Follow the RA even if it conflicts with ATC instructions, then inform ATC as soon as practicable.
Land immediately.
Switch off the transponder.
items.explanation: TCAS/ACAS RAs have priority for collision avoidance; ATC must be informed after compliance.

items.question: What is a limitation regarding use of night vision imaging systems (NVIS/NVG) in the AW139, when installed?
options: They may be used without any training.
They require specific crew training, procedures and aircraft configuration approval.
They are permitted only in day VMC.
They replace all need for external lighting.
items.explanation: NVIS operations require dedicated approvals, aircraft configuration and trained crews.

items.question: What is the crew requirement regarding altimeter setting procedures (QNH/QFE/STD) when using the AW139 in IFR?
options: Any setting is acceptable.
Procedures from the operations manual and state rules must be followed, including transition altitude/level practices.
Only QFE may be used.
Only QNH may be used above FL100.
items.explanation: Altimeter setting procedures must comply with state rules and the operator's manual, ensuring correct use of QNH/QFE/STD and transition criteria.

items.question: What must be considered when using the AW139 autopilot in turbulence?
options: Autopilot may always be used with no restrictions.
Manufacturer and AFCS limitations regarding turbulence may restrict use of some modes or require manual flying.
Autopilot must always be disengaged in smooth air.
Autopilot is prohibited below 5000 ft.
items.explanation: AFCS limitations can restrict autopilot use in severe turbulence; pilots must apply the RFM and operations manual guidance.

items.question: Which crew check is important before relying on navigation indications from VOR/ILS receivers on the AW139?
options: That cabin lights are on.
That the correct frequency and course are set and ident tones confirm the tuned facility.
That fuel pumps are off.
That the rotor brake is released.
items.explanation: Correct tuning, course selection and positive identification of the facility are required before relying on VOR/ILS indications.

items.question: When operating in RVSM airspace (if applicable to the AW139), what is a key avionics requirement?
options: Only a single altimeter is required.
Certified altimetry system performance and redundancy as specified in RVSM rules.
No transponder is needed.
Only GPS is required.
items.explanation: RVSM operations require specific certified altimetry system performance and redundancy.

items.question: How should the crew treat MEL/DDG limitations affecting avionics or AFCS equipment on the AW139?
options: They may be ignored if weather is good.
They must be complied with; dispatch is allowed only if the MEL permits it for the given defect.
They apply only to maintenance staff.
They are recommendations only.
items.explanation: MEL/DDG provide binding dispatch conditions; avionics/AFCS defects must be assessed against these documents.

items.question: What is an important pilot action regarding COM radios when operating the AW139 under IFR?
options: Set radios randomly.
Ensure correct frequency selection, volume and monitoring of required ATC and guard frequencies per procedures.
Use only one COM radio at all times.
Turn off radios in IMC.
items.explanation: Correct tuning and monitoring of COM radios is essential for IFR operations and ATC communication.

items.question: What does a loss of all primary attitude and heading displays on the AW139 require from the crew?
options: Immediate landing gear extension.
Transition to use of standby instruments and appropriate abnormal procedures.
No specific action.
Engine shutdown.
items.explanation: Loss of primary displays requires use of standby instruments and adherence to abnormal procedures for continued safe flight and landing.
